What Is Science?

" + "

Science is the systematic study of the natural world through observation, experimentation, and reasoning. Scientists ask questions, form hypotheses, collect data, and draw conclusions based on evidence — not opinions or guesses.

" + "

The three main branches of science:

" + "
  • Life Science — the study of living things (biology)
  • Physical Science — the study of matter and energy (chemistry + physics)
  • Earth Science — the study of Earth and space (geology, meteorology, astronomy)
" + "

The Scientific Method

" + "

The scientific method is a step-by-step process scientists use to investigate questions. The steps are not always linear — scientists often loop back and revise.

" + "
  1. Ask a Question — What do you want to know?
  2. Research — What do you already know? What have others discovered?
  3. Form a Hypothesis — A testable prediction. If… then… because…
  4. Experiment — Design a controlled test.
  5. Collect Data — Record observations and measurements.
  6. Analyze Data — Look for patterns, calculate averages, make graphs.
  7. Draw Conclusions — Was your hypothesis supported or not?
  8. Communicate Results — Share findings with others.
" + "

Variables and Controls

" + "

Every good experiment has three types of variables:

" + "
  • Independent Variable (IV) — The one thing you change on purpose.
  • Dependent Variable (DV) — The thing you measure; it depends on the IV.
  • Control Variables (Constants) — Everything that stays the same.
" + "

Control Group: The group that does not receive the experimental treatment. Used for comparison. Example: A plant given no fertilizer while others get fertilizer.

" + "

Experimental Group: The group that receives the treatment.

" + "

Data and Graphing

" + "

Data comes in two flavors:

" + "
  • Qualitative Data — Descriptions. Uses your senses. (\"The liquid turned cloudy.\")
  • Quantitative Data — Numbers. Measurements. (\"The liquid reached 45°C.\")
" + "

Types of graphs:

" + "
  • Bar Graph — Comparing categories.
  • Line Graph — Showing change over time.
  • Pie Chart — Showing parts of a whole.
" + "

Rules for graphing: label both axes with units, give the graph a title like The Effect of [IV] on [DV], use a ruler. Neatness counts.

" + "

Example — Why Bread Gets Soggy

" + "Question: Why does my sandwich bread get soggy when I put sauce on it?

Background research: Bread is porous — it has tiny holes. Sauce has water in it. Water moves from wet things to dry things through a process called diffusion. The bread soaks up the water from the sauce. This is why the bread gets soggy.

Hypothesis: If I put sauce on bread and wait, then the bread will get soggy because the water in the sauce soaks into the bread.

Experiment: Take 3 slices of the same bread. Slice 1 gets no sauce (control). Slice 2 gets 1 tablespoon of sauce. Slice 3 gets 3 tablespoons of sauce. Wait 10 minutes. Measure how soggy each slice is by pressing a paper towel on it and seeing how much water comes off.

Data: Slice 1 — paper towel dry. Slice 2 — small wet spot. Slice 3 — big wet spot, bread falling apart.

Conclusion: The hypothesis was supported. More sauce = more sogginess. The water in the sauce soaks into the bread.

Real-world fix: Put a layer of something between the sauce and the bread — like lettuce, cheese, or butter. Butter is fat and fat blocks water. This is why people butter their bread before making a sandwich." + "

Vocabulary Review

" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "" + "
TermDefinition
ScienceThe systematic study of the natural world
HypothesisA testable prediction based on observations
Independent VariableThe variable the scientist changes on purpose
Dependent VariableThe variable that is measured
Control GroupThe group that receives no experimental treatment
ConstantA factor that stays the same in an experiment
DataInformation collected during an experiment
Qualitative DataDescriptive observations using the senses
Quantitative DataNumerical measurements
InferenceA logical conclusion based on evidence
ObservationInformation gathered using the five senses
TheoryA well-tested explanation supported by much evidence
LawA rule describing a pattern in nature
ModelA representation used to explain something
" + "

End of Chapter 1 notes. Additional reference material available via the button in the corner.
